_meta.description: Per-species field notes for the bird-id dex drill-down card. Santa Barbara, CA soundscape. Keyed by the slug used in birds.json. Seeded from a Gemini-written local-birding blurb, then fact-checked and expanded. Sound, habitat, season, and behavior are written to be accurate for coastal Southern California; nothing here is invented.

fields.group: Which part of the local soundscape this bird belongs to.
fields.season: Residency status in the Santa Barbara area.
fields.sound: What you actually hear — song and/or calls.
fields.habitat: Where in the area you're most likely to hear it.
fields.note: A field note: behavior, ID tip, or context worth knowing.

mourning_dove.sound: A soft, mournful coo-OO-oo-oo-oo that's often mistaken for an owl. Its wings produce a sharp whistling 'twitter' on takeoff and landing.
mourning_dove.habitat: Open yards, wires, fields, and woodland edges everywhere in town.
mourning_dove.note: One of the most abundant and widespread birds in North America. Pairs forage on the ground for seeds and raise multiple broods a year.

house_finch.sound: A long, bright, rambling warble that typically ends in a buzzy downward-slurred 'wheer.' Calls are a sweet rising 'cheep.'
house_finch.habitat: Feeders, rooftops, and shrubs in every neighborhood.
house_finch.note: Males show red on the head and breast; the red comes from pigments in their diet, so color varies from pale yellow to deep red.

annas_hummingbird.sound: A scratchy, buzzy, metallic song delivered from a high perch, plus an explosive 'pop' at the bottom of the male's J-shaped display dive — the pop is made by tail feathers, not the voice.
annas_hummingbird.habitat: Gardens, flowering shrubs, and feeders year-round.
annas_hummingbird.note: The only hummingbird that stays in the Santa Barbara area through winter in good numbers. Males flash a brilliant magenta head and throat.

turkey_vulture.sound: Essentially silent — only low hisses and grunts at the roost or nest. Detections labeled as this species are usually other sounds.
turkey_vulture.habitat: Soaring over foothills, fields, and the coast.
turkey_vulture.note: Identified by flight, not voice: it soars on raised, V-shaped wings and rocks side to side. Finds carrion largely by smell, unusual among birds.

california_towhee.sound: A sharp, metallic 'chink!' given from the ground or a low bush, often speeding into a rattling series. Pairs greet each other with a squealing duet.
california_towhee.habitat: Chaparral, garden edges, and brushy yards.
california_towhee.note: A plain warm-brown sparrow relative that scratches in leaf litter with a double-footed hop. Almost always seen on or near the ground.

california_scrub_jay.sound: A loud, harsh, rising 'shreenk!' and dry rattling series. Bold and noisy.
california_scrub_jay.habitat: Oak woodland, chaparral, and suburban yards.
california_scrub_jay.note: Blue above and gray-backed with no crest. Caches thousands of acorns each fall and remembers where — an important oak disperser.

common_raven.sound: A deep, throaty, resonant 'kronk' or croak — lower and more guttural than a crow's caw.
common_raven.habitat: Everywhere, from the coast to the backcountry; soars over ridgelines.
common_raven.note: Larger than a crow with a heavy bill, shaggy throat, and a wedge-shaped tail in flight. Among the most intelligent of all birds.

western_gull.sound: A loud, laughing 'kyow-kyow' and a long bugling call, plus 'kak-kak-kak' alarm notes that echo from the harbor and rooftops downtown.
western_gull.habitat: Coastline, harbor, beaches, and State Street.
western_gull.note: A large gull with a dark slate back and pink legs. Breeds on the Channel Islands and is the default 'seagull' of the Santa Barbara coast.

black_phoebe.sound: A sharp, rhythmic 'fi-bee, fi-bee' song and a sturdy 'tsip' call from a low perch.
black_phoebe.habitat: Near water — fountains, lawns, creeks, and pool edges.
black_phoebe.note: A crisp black flycatcher with a white belly that constantly pumps its tail. Sallies out to snap insects from the air and returns to its perch.

european_starling.sound: A bizarre medley of clicks, rattles, wheezes, and clear whistles, woven with dead-on imitations of other birds and even mechanical sounds.
european_starling.habitat: Lawns, parking lots, and tree cavities throughout town.
european_starling.note: Introduced to North America in the 1890s. Glossy and iridescent up close; gathers in large flocks and competes with native cavity-nesters.

cliff_swallow.sound: A squeaky, grating chatter and twittering, given around the colony.
cliff_swallow.habitat: Over open ground and water; nests on bridges, overpasses, and building eaves.
cliff_swallow.note: Builds enclosed gourd-shaped mud nests in dense colonies. Square tail and pale rump separate it from the fork-tailed Barn Swallow.

eurasian_collared_dove.sound: A three-note 'coo-COO-cup' with the stress in the middle — flatter and more mechanical than the Mourning Dove's mournful coo. In flight it gives a harsh nasal 'hwaa.'
eurasian_collared_dove.note: Pale gray with a thin black half-collar on the nape. Spread across North America from the 1980s after escaping in the Caribbean.

song_sparrow.sound: A bright musical song that usually opens with two or three clear notes, then breaks into a jumble of trills and buzzes. Call is a nasal 'chimp.'
song_sparrow.habitat: Brushy edges, marshes, gardens, and creeksides.
song_sparrow.note: Heavily streaked brown with a dark central spot on the breast. Among the most variable songsters in North America — local birds learn regional song dialects.

mallard.sound: The classic loud, descending 'quack' is the female; the male gives a quieter, raspy 'rhab.'
mallard.habitat: Ponds, lagoons, creeks, and park lakes.
mallard.note: The familiar dabbling duck — green-headed male, mottled-brown female. Tips forward to feed on submerged plants and is the ancestor of most domestic ducks.

california_quail.sound: A loud, rhythmic three-note assembly call that sounds like 'chi-CA-go!' Coveys also keep up soft contact clucks.
california_quail.habitat: Chaparral, brushy slopes, and garden edges near cover.
california_quail.note: California's state bird, with a forward-curling teardrop head plume. Travels in family coveys that sprint for cover rather than fly when alarmed.

wilsons_warbler.sound: A rapid, chattering trill that drops in pitch and speeds up toward the end ('chi-chi-chi-chet-chet').
wilsons_warbler.habitat: Willow and riparian thickets, shaded canyon undergrowth.
wilsons_warbler.note: A small, bright yellow warbler; the male wears a neat round black cap. Active and twitchy, often flicking its tail as it gleans insects.

red_tailed_hawk.sound: A fierce, raspy, descending scream — 'keeeee-arr' — famous as the stock 'eagle' or 'hawk' sound dubbed into films.
red_tailed_hawk.habitat: Soaring over open country, foothills, and freeways; perches on poles and snags.
red_tailed_hawk.note: The default large soaring hawk of the region. Adults show a brick-red tail above. Hunts rodents and reptiles from a perch or while circling.

red_shouldered_hawk.sound: A loud, clear, repeated screaming whistle — often written as 'kee-ah' or 'kee-yar' — delivered in a steady series, especially when defending a territory. One of the most vocal local raptors; often heard before it is seen.
red_shouldered_hawk.habitat: Riparian corridors, oak woodland, and neighborhoods with tall mature trees — especially near creeks and canyon bottoms.
red_shouldered_hawk.note: Coastal California birds are the western subspecies (B. l. elegans): rufous-barred breast, black-and-white banded tail, and in flight a pale crescent near each wingtip. Hunts from a perch — mice, frogs, snakes, and other small prey.

nuttalls_woodpecker.sound: A rolling, descending rattle and a sharp 'pit' or 'pidik' call. Drums in short bursts on dead wood.
nuttalls_woodpecker.note: A small black-and-white 'ladder-backed' woodpecker nearly endemic to California. The male has a red crown patch.

american_crow.sound: The familiar loud, harsh 'caw-caw.' Highly varied — also rattles, clicks, and a softer 'awk.'
american_crow.habitat: Neighborhoods, parks, fields, and trash everywhere.
american_crow.note: Smaller than a raven with a fan-shaped tail and even 'caw.' Very social and intelligent; family groups forage and roost together.

wrentit.sound: The 'voice of the chaparral' — a series of clear ringing 'pit' notes that accelerate into a trill like a bouncing ping-pong ball (the female's version stays even and doesn't speed up).
wrentit.note: Far more often heard than seen. A small, drab, long-tailed skulker with a pale eye, famously sedentary — many spend their whole lives within a few acres.

bushtit.sound: A constant, high-pitched, gossipy patter of tiny 'tsit-tsit' contact notes as a flock drifts through the foliage.
bushtit.note: A tiny, plain gray bird with a long tail that travels in restless flocks. Weaves a remarkable hanging, sock-shaped nest from spiderweb and lichen.

brown_pelican.sound: Adults are essentially silent away from the colony; nestlings are noisy. Detections of this species are usually other sounds.
brown_pelican.note: Identified by sight: it plunge-dives headfirst for fish. Recovered from near-extinction after the DDT era; breeds on the Channel Islands.

lesser_goldfinch.sound: A sweet, wheezy, frantic jumble of whistles that often borrows phrases from other birds, plus a plaintive falling 'tee-yee.'
lesser_goldfinch.note: A tiny finch — males are greenish-yellow with a black cap. An accomplished mimic that works snippets of other species into its song.

northern_mockingbird.sound: A tireless performer that strings together imitations of other birds, car alarms, and insects, repeating each phrase three or more times before moving on. Unmated males sing day and night in spring.
northern_mockingbird.habitat: Suburban yards, hedges, and parking lots.
northern_mockingbird.note: Gray with bold white wing patches that flash in flight and in its wing-flashing display. Fiercely defends its territory.

spotted_towhee.sound: A buzzy, mechanical trill and a rising, cat-like 'mew' call from inside dense cover.
spotted_towhee.habitat: Chaparral, brushy thickets, and woodland understory.
spotted_towhee.note: A striking towhee with a black hood, rufous sides, and white-spotted back and red eyes. Noisily double-scratches in leaf litter.

brewers_blackbird.sound: A harsh 'check' and a creaky, rising whistle.
brewers_blackbird.habitat: Lawns, parking lots, fields, and outdoor dining areas.
brewers_blackbird.note: Males are glossy black with a pale staring eye; females are plain gray-brown. Struts confidently on the ground around people.

pacific_slope_flycatcher.sound: A sharp, rising, squeaky 'pseet?' or 'tseweep' from a shaded perch.
pacific_slope_flycatcher.habitat: Cool, shaded canyon bottoms and riparian woodland.
pacific_slope_flycatcher.note: A small olive flycatcher with a teardrop eyering, best told from look-alikes by voice. Sallies for insects in the understory.

double_crested_cormorant.sound: Mostly silent; gives low, pig-like grunts at colonies. Detections are usually other sounds.
double_crested_cormorant.note: Swims low in the water and dives to chase fish. Often perches with wings spread to dry, since its feathers aren't fully waterproof.

red_winged_blackbird.sound: The male's gurgling, liquid 'conk-la-ree!' delivered from a cattail, plus a sharp 'check' call.
red_winged_blackbird.habitat: Freshwater marshes, lagoon edges, and reedbeds.
red_winged_blackbird.note: Glossy black males flare scarlet-and-yellow shoulder patches to display; females are streaky brown and sparrow-like. Nests in loose marsh colonies.

bewicks_wren.sound: A loud, remarkably varied song that opens with sharp notes and ends in a musical buzzy trill — repertoires differ bird to bird.
bewicks_wren.habitat: Brushy thickets, chaparral, and garden tangles.
bewicks_wren.note: A small brown wren with a bold white eyebrow and a long tail it flicks side to side. Inquisitive and vocal, it often scolds from cover.

oak_titmouse.sound: A scratchy, scolding 'tsick-a-dee' and a clear, whistled 'peter-peter-peter.'
oak_titmouse.note: A plain gray bird with a small pointed crest — 'a bird without a field mark.' Pairs hold territory year-round in the oaks they depend on.

brown_headed_cowbird.sound: The male's liquid, bubbling 'glug-glug-gleee' followed by thin, high whistles.
brown_headed_cowbird.habitat: Open lawns, field edges, and feeders.
brown_headed_cowbird.note: A brood parasite: females lay eggs in other birds' nests and leave them to raise the young. Males are black with a brown head.

acorn_woodpecker.sound: A loud, chaotic, laughing 'waka-waka-waka' that echoes through oak groves.
acorn_woodpecker.note: A clown-faced, social woodpecker that drills 'granary' trees with thousands of holes to store acorns. Lives in cooperative family groups.

killdeer.sound: A loud, piercing, insistent 'kill-deer! kill-deer!' often given in flight or while running.
killdeer.habitat: Lawns, ballfields, gravel lots, and open ground — not just shorelines.
killdeer.note: A plover with two black breast bands. Famous for its broken-wing act, feigning injury to lure predators away from its ground nest.

black_headed_grosbeak.sound: A rich, rolling, robin-like warble — sweeter and more fluid than an American Robin's. Call is a sharp 'eek' or 'spik.'
black_headed_grosbeak.habitat: Oak and riparian woodland, leafy neighborhoods.
black_headed_grosbeak.note: A chunky songbird with a heavy pale bill; the male is burnt-orange with a black head. Both sexes sing, and it's one of the few birds that can safely eat toxic monarch butterflies.

house_sparrow.sound: A monotonous, endless 'cheep' and 'chirrup' chorus from hedges and eaves.
house_sparrow.habitat: Buildings, outdoor dining, and strip malls.
house_sparrow.note: An Old World species introduced to North America in the 1850s. Tied closely to people; males have a black bib and gray cap.

barn_swallow.sound: A liquid, twittering warble interspersed with a sharp 'vit' and a mechanical buzz.
barn_swallow.habitat: Over open fields, water, and around barns and buildings.
barn_swallow.note: The most widespread swallow in the world. Steely blue above and buff below with a deeply forked tail; builds an open mud cup on ledges and eaves.

allens_hummingbird.sound: Thin, buzzy chip notes; the male's wings produce a buzz, and his display dive ends with a metallic sputter.
allens_hummingbird.habitat: Coastal scrub, canyon edges, and gardens.
allens_hummingbird.note: Very similar to a tiny Rufous Hummingbird, with a green back and rufous flanks. The migratory form arrives early (winter) to breed along the coast and largely departs by late summer.

ash_throated_flycatcher.sound: A rolling 'ka-brick' and a burry 'prrrt,' often given at dawn.
ash_throated_flycatcher.habitat: Dry oak woodland, chaparral, and arid scrub.
ash_throated_flycatcher.note: A slim flycatcher with a pale gray throat, lemon belly, and rusty tail. Nests in tree cavities and even fenceposts or pipes.

orange_crowned_warbler.season: Year-round along the coast; most vocal in spring
orange_crowned_warbler.sound: A soft, rapid trill that loses energy and drops in pitch at the very end.
orange_crowned_warbler.habitat: Chaparral, riparian thickets, and garden shrubs.
orange_crowned_warbler.note: A plain yellow-olive warbler with few marks; the orange crown is almost never visible. Coastal Southern California is one of the few places it can be found in winter.

bullocks_oriole.sound: A series of bright, staccato whistles punctuated by harsh, chattering rattles.
bullocks_oriole.habitat: Riparian and oak woodland, tall shade trees.
bullocks_oriole.note: The male is flame-orange with a black cap, eyeline, and throat and a bold white wing patch. Weaves a hanging pouch nest near the tips of branches.

american_coot.sound: A noisy assortment of clucks, grunts, croaks, and cackles.
american_coot.note: A slaty waterbird that looks duck-like but isn't — it has a white chicken-like bill and lobed (not webbed) toes. Patters across the water to take off.

western_kingbird.sound: A sharp, squeaky, bickering chatter — 'kit-kit-keer' — often from a wire.
western_kingbird.habitat: Open country, field edges, and roadside wires.
western_kingbird.note: A bold gray-and-yellow flycatcher with a black tail edged in white. Aggressively chases hawks and ravens out of its territory.

western_bluebird.sound: A soft, mellow 'few' or 'chew' call and a quiet, chuckling song.
western_bluebird.habitat: Open oak woodland, parks, and pasture edges.
western_bluebird.note: The male is deep blue with a rusty breast. Nests in tree cavities and readily uses nest boxes; hunts insects by dropping to the ground from a low perch.

common_yellowthroat.sound: A rolling, rhythmic 'witchety-witchety-witchety' song and a husky 'chuck' call from the reeds.
common_yellowthroat.habitat: Freshwater marshes, lagoon edges, and damp thickets.
common_yellowthroat.note: A small warbler; the male wears a black 'bandit' mask. Skulks low in dense marsh vegetation, popping up to sing.

caspian_tern.sound: A loud, harsh, grating 'kraaaa,' often given overhead.
caspian_tern.note: The world's largest tern, with a heavy blood-red bill and black cap. Hovers and plunge-dives for fish.

great_egret.sound: A low, harsh croak, usually only when disturbed or at the colony.
great_egret.habitat: Marshes, lagoons, tidal flats, and pond edges.
great_egret.note: A tall, all-white heron with a yellow bill and black legs. Stalks slowly in the shallows, then spears fish with a quick thrust. Plume hunting nearly wiped it out a century ago.

great_blue_heron.sound: A deep, harsh, croaking 'frahnk' squawk when flushed.
great_blue_heron.habitat: Lagoons, creeks, tidal flats, and even golf courses.
great_blue_heron.note: The largest heron in North America — tall and blue-gray. Stands motionless in the shallows waiting to strike at fish, frogs, and gophers.

rock_pigeon.sound: A soft, throaty cooing 'coo-roo-coo'; wings clap on takeoff.
rock_pigeon.habitat: Downtown ledges, bridges, plazas, and parking structures.
rock_pigeon.note: The familiar city pigeon, descended from wild Rock Doves of Europe and brought over centuries ago. Plumage ranges widely from gray to white to rusty.

california_gull.sound: A laughing, bugling call and 'kak-kak' notes, similar to other gulls.
california_gull.habitat: Beaches, harbor, parking lots, and landfills.
california_gull.note: A medium gull with yellow-green legs and a red-and-black spot on the bill. Breeds at inland lakes to the north and east, then winters along the California coast.

dark_eyed_junco.sound: A rapid, musical, ringing trill on one pitch, plus sharp 'tick' or 'tek' call notes.
dark_eyed_junco.habitat: Suburban yards, woodland edges, and feeders.
dark_eyed_junco.note: The local 'Oregon' form has a dark hood, brown back, and pinkish sides; white outer tail feathers flash as it flies up. Forages on the ground with a tidy hop.

barn_owl.sound: Not a hooter — gives a harsh, drawn-out, raspy shriek or scream, plus hisses and snores at the nest.
barn_owl.habitat: Open grassland, farmland, palms, and old buildings; hunts low over fields at night.
barn_owl.note: A pale, ghostly owl with a heart-shaped facial disk and dark eyes. Hunts almost entirely by sound, locating rodents in total darkness, and readily uses nest boxes.

great_horned_owl.sound: A deep, soft, rhythmic series of hoots — 'hoo-h'HOO-hoo-hoo' — often answered by a mate in a lower-and-higher duet.
great_horned_owl.habitat: Oak woodland, canyon edges, parks, and tall trees near open ground.
great_horned_owl.note: A large, powerful owl with prominent feather 'ear' tufts and yellow eyes. The region's top nocturnal predator; nests early in winter, often reusing an old hawk or raven nest.

white_breasted_nuthatch.sound: A nasal, repeated 'yank-yank-yank,' lower and more drawn-out than a chickadee.
white_breasted_nuthatch.habitat: Oak woodland and tall mature trees.
white_breasted_nuthatch.note: A compact blue-gray bird with a white face and black cap that creeps headfirst down tree trunks, prying insects and seeds from the bark.

brown_creeper.sound: A very high, thin, sibilant song ('trees-trees-see-the-trees') and a single high 'see' call — so high-pitched many people can't hear it.
brown_creeper.habitat: Mature oak and conifer woodland with large trunks.
brown_creeper.note: A tiny, bark-colored bird that spirals up a tree trunk probing crevices for insects, then drops to the base of the next tree to start over. Easily overlooked against the bark.

white_crowned_sparrow.sound: A clear whistle followed by buzzy, trilled notes, with distinct local dialects; call is a sharp metallic 'pink.'
white_crowned_sparrow.habitat: Brushy edges, weedy fields, gardens, and hedgerows.
white_crowned_sparrow.note: A crisp gray sparrow; adults wear bold black-and-white crown stripes (immatures are brown-and-tan). Forages on the ground in winter flocks, then heads far north and to the mountains to breed.

green_winged_teal.sound: The male gives a clear, high, whistled 'preep'; the female a thin quack.
green_winged_teal.habitat: Ponds, lagoon edges, marshes, and shallow mudflats.
green_winged_teal.note: The smallest dabbling duck in North America. The male has a chestnut head with a green eye-patch and a vertical white bar on the side; winters here and breeds far to the north.

western_grebe.sound: A high, rolling, two-note 'creet-creet' that carries across the water.
western_grebe.note: A large, elegant black-and-white waterbird with a long slender neck and a long yellow bill. Dives for fish and is famous for the synchronized 'rushing' courtship dance across the surface.

forsters_tern.sound: A low, nasal, grating 'kerr' that drops in pitch.
forsters_tern.habitat: Harbor, lagoons, estuaries, and the open coast.
forsters_tern.note: A pale medium-sized tern; nonbreeding birds show a black 'mask' through the eye rather than a full cap. Hovers and plunge-dives for small fish.

whimbrel.sound: A rippling, even series of short whistles, all on one pitch — 'pip-pip-pip-pip-pip-pip-pip.'
whimbrel.habitat: Beaches, rocky shores, tidal flats, and mudflats.
whimbrel.note: A large brown shorebird with a long, smoothly downcurved bill and a striped crown. Probes mud and pries crabs from rocks; a long-distance migrant along the coast.

american_goldfinch.sound: A bright, lively, rambling song of sweet whistled notes, trills, and twitters delivered in a bouncy rhythm. In flight, it gives a distinctive, cheerful 'po-ta-to-chip!' call.
american_goldfinch.habitat: Riparian edges, weedy fields, gardens, and backyard feeders.
american_goldfinch.note: Males are brilliant yellow with a black cap and wings in summer; females and winter birds are a drab olive-brown. While the similar Lesser Goldfinch is ubiquitous year-round in Santa Barbara yards, American Goldfinches are more localized and are often detected visiting feeders in winter and spring flocks. With only a single low-confidence detection on record, backyard mic IDs can be noisy, but the species is highly plausible locally.

band_tailed_pigeon.sound: A deep, hollow, two-syllable cooing that sounds owl-like: 'hoo-whoo' or 'whoo-hoo', repeated slowly. Wings produce a loud, sharp clapping sound upon takeoff.
band_tailed_pigeon.habitat: Oak woodlands, foothill canyons, and residential yards with mature trees.
band_tailed_pigeon.note: Our native wild pigeon, much larger and sleeker than a Mourning Dove, with a yellow bill, yellow feet, and a white crescent on the back of the neck. They travel in nomadic flocks searching out acorns and berries, and can suddenly appear in large numbers in foothill yards before vanishing.

black_crowned_night_heron.sound: A sudden, loud, harsh, flat croak or 'quok' that is often heard at dusk or during the night as they fly overhead.
black_crowned_night_heron.habitat: Lagoons, harbors, creeks, marshes, and roosting in tall trees near water.
black_crowned_night_heron.note: A stocky, short-necked heron with a black back, gray wings, and long white head plumes in breeding plumage. Strictly nocturnal or crepuscular, they spend the day hunched silently in dense foliage near water before emerging at dusk to hunt fish, frogs, and crustaceans.

canada_goose.sound: A loud, resonant, musical honking 'ah-honk' or 'ka-ronk', often given in flight by V-shaped flocks.
canada_goose.habitat: Lakes, parks, golf courses, estuaries, and lawns near water.
canada_goose.note: The familiar large goose with a black head and neck, white 'chinstrap,' and brown body. While wild flocks migrate through in winter, feral resident populations are present year-round in local parks and golf courses. With only a single low-confidence detection on record, this was likely a flyover or a local park bird.

cedar_waxwing.sound: High-pitched, thin, sibilant trills or whistles: a soft, high 'zeee' or 'bzeee' that is easily overlooked.
cedar_waxwing.habitat: Residential yards with fruiting trees, parks, and riparian corridors.
cedar_waxwing.note: Sleek, crested, silky-brown birds with a black mask and bright yellow tail tip. They travel in highly social, nomadic flocks that descend on berry-producing trees and shrubs like pyracantha and toyon, stripping them bare before moving on.

chestnut_backed_chickadee.sound: A scratchy, high-pitched 'tseek-a-dee-dee' or 'chick-a-dee' call, faster and squeakier than other chickadees. They do not have a whistled song.
chestnut_backed_chickadee.habitat: Shady oak woodlands, riparian canyons, and mature residential yards.
chestnut_backed_chickadee.note: A small, active bird with a rich chestnut back and flanks, a black cap, and white cheeks. Santa Barbara is near the southern limit of their range, where they are increasingly common in shady yards and oak groves, often foraging in mixed flocks with bushtits and warblers.

coopers_hawk.sound: A rapid, nasal, barking series of 'kak-kak-kak-kak' calls, usually given near the nest in spring. Mostly silent during the rest of the year.
coopers_hawk.habitat: Oak woodlands, riparian corridors, and leafy residential neighborhoods.
coopers_hawk.note: A medium-sized, agile forest hawk with a long banded tail and rounded wings. It has adapted well to suburban Santa Barbara, where it frequently hunts songbirds around backyard feeders. With only a single low-confidence detection on record, backyard mic IDs can be noisy, but the species is highly plausible locally.

downy_woodpecker.sound: A sharp, flat 'pik' call and a high-pitched, descending whinny or rattle. Drums on dead wood in rapid, even taps.
downy_woodpecker.habitat: Riparian woodlands, willow thickets, and mature suburban trees.
downy_woodpecker.note: The smallest woodpecker in North America, black-and-white with a small bill. It is uncommon in coastal Santa Barbara, where the very similar Nuttall's Woodpecker is the default resident. Low-confidence backyard detections should be treated with caution, as they are easily confused with Nuttall's Woodpecker calls or drum patterns.

house_wren.sound: A fast, bubbling, liquid song that rises in pitch and intensity, then cascades downward in a sweet, chattering torrent. Also a harsh, scolding 'churr.'
house_wren.habitat: Oak woodlands, riparian edges, and brushy residential yards with nesting cavities.
house_wren.note: A small, plain brown wren with faint dark barring on its wings and tail, lacking the bold white eyebrow of the Bewick's Wren. Highly energetic and territorial, they readily use nest boxes. With only a couple of low-confidence detections on record, backyard mic IDs can be noisy, but the species is highly plausible locally.

huttons_vireo.sound: A persistent, monotonous, two-note whistled song, typically 'zu-weep, zu-weep' or 'che-veek, che-veek', repeated endlessly. Also a dry, scolding rattle.
huttons_vireo.habitat: Oak woodlands, shaded canyons, and oak-shaded residential yards.
huttons_vireo.note: Superficially identical to a Ruby-crowned Kinglet, but has a thicker, slightly hooked bill, stouter blue-gray legs, and lacks the kinglet's constant wing-flicking. It is a classic oak canopy specialist and a very active vocalist in Santa Barbara's oak-dominated residential neighborhoods.

mountain_chickadee.season: Year-round resident (high elevations); rare winter visitor to coast
mountain_chickadee.sound: A clear, whistled, descending song: 'fee-bee-bay' or 'cheeseburger'. Also a scratchy 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee' call with a distinct husky quality.
mountain_chickadee.habitat: Conifer forests at high elevations; occasionally oak woodlands or yards during winter downslope movements.
mountain_chickadee.note: Distinguished from the Chestnut-backed Chickadee by its gray back, pale flanks, and a prominent white eyebrow stripe cutting through its black cap. Detections on coastal backyard mics are highly unusual and may represent downslope winter wanderers, or potentially acoustic misidentifications of other species.

mountain_quail.sound: A loud, clear, echoing, single-note whistled 'plook!' or 'que-ark!' given at intervals of several seconds in spring.
mountain_quail.habitat: Dense chaparral, montane scrub, and steep foothill slopes.
mountain_quail.note: Larger than the California Quail, with a long, straight, vertical head plume and chestnut throat and flanks with bold white bars. They are secretive residents of the high chaparral and montane slopes, rarely descending to coastal yards. Backyard detections are likely foothill residents or potential acoustic misidentifications of other loud, sharp sounds.

northern_rough_winged_swallow.sound: A short, flat, buzzy, unmusical 'bzzzt' or 'vrt' call, given in flight. Lacks the sweet, liquid twittering of other swallows.
northern_rough_winged_swallow.habitat: Over creeks, lagoons, coastal cliffs, and open fields.
northern_rough_winged_swallow.note: A plain brown-backed swallow with a dingy throat and white belly. They nest in burrows along dirt banks, drainpipes, or crevices in bridges. With only a single low-confidence detection on record, this was likely a spring migrant or summer foraging visitor.

purple_finch.sound: A rich, fast, musical, rolling warble, sweeter and more continuous than the House Finch's song, without the buzzy downward 'wheer' ending. Call is a flat, metallic 'pit.'
purple_finch.habitat: Moist oak woodlands, coniferous forests, and foothill yards.
purple_finch.note: Males are a raspberry-red (often described as 'dipped in cranberry juice'), while females are heavily streaked with a bold white eyebrow. They are easily confused with the ubiquitous House Finch; in coastal Santa Barbara, they are mostly winter downslope visitors, though they breed in the nearby mountains.

rock_wren.sound: A highly varied, mechanical song consisting of distinct, repeated phrases — 'che-ree, che-ree, che-ree, trrrrrr, tew-tew-tew' — with a dry, buzzing quality. Call is a dry, buzzy 'tick-ear.'
rock_wren.habitat: Rocky canyons, dry slopes, road cuts, and stony washes in the foothills.
rock_wren.note: A pale gray-brown wren with a finely speckled back and a buffy rump. They are highly specialized for rocky terrain and are uncommon in flat residential yards. With only a single low-confidence detection on record, this was likely a foothill wanderer or an acoustic misidentification.

rufous_hummingbird.sound: Buzzy chip notes and a high, metallic, squealing chatter. The male's wings produce a high-pitched, musical hum in flight.
rufous_hummingbird.habitat: Gardens, flowering chaparral, and feeders during migration.
rufous_hummingbird.note: Famous for its aggressive nature, the male is brilliant coppery-orange, while females and immatures have green backs and rufous flanks. They do not breed locally but pass through Santa Barbara in spring (February–April) and fall (July–September), often taking over backyard feeders. With only a single low-confidence detection on record, backyard mic IDs can be noisy, but the species is highly plausible during migration.

stellers_jay.season: Year-round resident (mountains); occasional winter visitor to coast
stellers_jay.sound: A harsh, nasal, repeated 'shack-sheek-sheek' or 'wah-wah-wah' scold. Also an expert mimic, frequently giving a flawless imitation of a Red-tailed Hawk's scream.
stellers_jay.habitat: Conifer and high oak forests in the mountains; occasionally wanders to foothill yards.
stellers_jay.note: A striking, crested jay, deep blue with a black head and shoulders. They are residents of the higher, wetter mountain forests of Santa Barbara County and are rare in coastal lowlands. With only a single low-confidence detection on record, this was likely a mountain bird or an acoustic misidentification.

western_tanager.sound: A short, hoarse, robin-like song of rising and falling phrases, with a distinctly buzzy or raspy quality. Call is a dry, three-note 'pit-er-ick.'
western_tanager.habitat: Oak canopy, riparian corridors, and leafy suburban yards during migration.
western_tanager.note: The male is a spectacular sight with a flame-orange head, bright yellow body, and black wings and tail. They are common spring migrants in Santa Barbara (April–May) as they travel to montane breeding grounds, often foraging high in oak and sycamore canopies.

wild_turkey.sound: The male's loud, echoing 'gobble-gobble-gobble,' plus dry, sharp 'clucks' and 'putts' given by both sexes.
wild_turkey.habitat: Oak savannas, grasslands, and foothill ranchlands.
wild_turkey.note: A massive, heavy-bodied bird introduced to California for hunting. While common in the Santa Ynez Valley and backcountry, they are rare on the coastal side of the mountains. With only a single low-confidence detection on record, backyard mic IDs near the coast can be noisy, and this was likely a misidentified loud noise or a rare foothill wanderer.
